Extensive describes something that is large in scope, range, or coverage — something that spreads widely, covers a lot of ground, or includes a great many things.

Think of it this way: if you lay a blanket over a large area to cover as much of the ground as possible, the coverage is extensive. The blanket stretches widely and touches many parts of the ground. That "wide stretch" or "large coverage" is at the heart of what extensive means.

The word is remarkably flexible. It can describe:

Physical space — land, buildings, or areas that cover a large stretch.

  • "The king owned extensive lands across the country." (The lands spread over a very large area.)
  • "The hospital has an extensive network of underground tunnels."

Knowledge or learning — when someone has studied or learned about a wide range of things.

  • "She has extensive knowledge of ancient history." (She knows a lot, and her knowledge covers many areas within that subject.)
  • "He received extensive training before becoming a pilot."

Research, investigation, or effort — when work goes deeply and widely into a subject.

  • "Scientists conducted extensive research before releasing the drug." (They tested it thoroughly, over many experiments and conditions.)
  • "The police launched an extensive search for the missing child."

Damage or harm — when destruction or injury affects a large portion of something.

  • "The earthquake caused extensive damage to the city." (Many buildings, roads, and areas were damaged — not just one spot.)
  • "The patient had extensive injuries to the chest and abdomen."

Collections, libraries, or lists — when something includes a large variety of items.

  • "The museum has an extensive collection of medieval art."
  • "The restaurant offers an extensive menu with over 80 dishes."

Experience or connections — when someone has been through many situations or knows many people.

  • "She has extensive experience in managing large teams."
  • "He has an extensive network of contacts in the business world."
The Key Idea: Breadth, Not Just Size

This is the most important thing to understand about extensive. It doesn't simply mean "big" or "large" in a general sense. It specifically refers to how widely or broadly something spreads or covers.

Compare:

  • A mountain is large or tall, but you would not call it extensive.
  • A forest that stretches for hundreds of kilometres in every direction? That is extensive — because it covers a vast area.

In the same way:

  • A person might know a lot about one narrow topic (say, one specific chemical reaction). That is deep knowledge, but not necessarily extensive knowledge.
  • A person who knows a lot across many different topics or areas — from history to science to literature — has extensive knowledge.

So the soul of the word is width and coverage, the idea of spreading out broadly rather than just being large in one dimension.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Extensive vs. comprehensive
Comprehensive means "covering everything — complete and leaving nothing out." Extensive means "covering a large range," but not necessarily every single part. An extensive report might cover many things; a comprehensive report covers everything relevant, with no gaps. Comprehensive has a sense of completeness; extensive has a sense of breadth.

Extensive vs. thorough
Thorough focuses on depth and care — doing something carefully and in detail without skipping steps. Extensive focuses on breadth — how wide the coverage is. You can do an extensive but not very thorough job (covering many things quickly), or a thorough but not very extensive job (going very deep into one specific thing).

Extensive vs. vast
Vast emphasises an overwhelming, almost immeasurable size — usually for physical space. The vast ocean. The vast universe. Extensive is more versatile; it applies to abstract things like knowledge, research, and experience just as comfortably as to physical space.

Extensive vs. broad
These are quite similar. Broad simply means "wide." Extensive carries the additional sense of scale and magnitude — it sounds more impressive. "A broad knowledge" and "an extensive knowledge" both work, but extensive suggests that the range is particularly large and noteworthy.

Extensive vs. intensive
These two are almost opposites in spirit, even though they sound related. Intensive means concentrated, focused, and high-effort in a small or specific area. Extensive means spread out widely. An intensive language course focuses hard on one language in a short time. Extensive reading in a language means reading widely across many books and topics over time.
Sentences That Show It in Action

Here are more examples to let the word sink in naturally:

  • "She spent years doing extensive reading before writing the book." (She read widely — many books, articles, and sources.)
  • "The fire caused extensive destruction to the old neighbourhood." (Many streets and buildings were affected.)
  • "The new software went through extensive testing before its release." (It was tested across many scenarios, systems, and conditions.)
  • "He has made extensive use of data to support his argument." (He used data in many parts of his argument, in many ways.)
  • "After an extensive search, the explorers finally found the ruins." (They searched over a wide area for a long time.)
  • "The doctor recommended extensive physical therapy for recovery." (Many sessions covering many types of exercises over a long period.)
  • "The journalist conducted extensive interviews across twenty countries." (She interviewed many people in many places.)

Extensive is a neutral word in itself — it simply describes scale and coverage. However, depending on context, it can sound:

Positive or impressive — when referring to effort, knowledge, or preparation.

  • "She has extensive experience." → This is a compliment; it sounds impressive.
  • "Extensive research was done." → This builds trust and credibility.

Serious or concerning — when referring to damage, injury, or loss.

  • "The flood caused extensive damage." → Here the word signals seriousness, not a positive thing.
  • "He suffered extensive injuries." → The scale of the harm is large.

The word itself doesn't have a built-in good or bad feeling — it simply tells you that the scale is large and the spread is wide. Whether that is good or bad comes from the noun it describes.
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar)

Extensive is an adjective, so it is always used to describe a noun.

You can place it:

Before the noun (most common):

  • extensive knowledge, extensive research, extensive damage

After a linking verb (like is, was, became, seems):

  • "The damage was extensive."
  • "Her experience is extensive."
  • "The repairs will be extensive."

You can also compare:

  • "Her knowledge is more extensive than his."
  • "This is the most extensive study ever done on the subject."
  • "The second storm caused fairly extensive damage."

If you want to remember extensive forever, hold onto this thought:

Something is extensive when it covers a wide range, a large area, or many parts of something — when it stretches broadly and includes a great deal.

When you hear extensive, think of something spreading out wide — like a large net cast over many waters, or a detailed map covering a whole continent. Whether it is knowledge, experience, research, damage, or physical space — if it is extensive, it is large in breadth and coverage.
